nameStory: The garden dahlia gets its name from Swedish botanist Anders Dahl, who lived in the 18th century and was a student of the famous Carl Linnaeus. The 'garden' part distinguishes it from its wild relatives, emphasizing that this showy flower has been bred and cultivated specifically for our flower beds and borders.
description: Garden dahlias are spectacular flowering plants that have become beloved additions to New England gardens, though they're not native to our region. These tender perennials grow from underground tubers and can range from compact 1-foot plants to towering 6-foot giants. They're famous for their incredibly diverse flower forms - from simple daisy-like blooms to elaborate pompoms, dinner-plate sized giants, and intricate cactus-shaped varieties in nearly every color except true blue.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Complex flower heads made up of many small flowers packed together, typical of the sunflower family. What look like petals are actually individual ray flowers surrounding a center of tiny disc flowers. The variety is endless - from 2-inch singles to 12-inch dinner plates, in colors from white through yellow, orange, red, purple, and nearly black.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Divided into leaflets (pinnate), giving them a somewhat ferny appearance. The leaves feel slightly rough and are typically deep green. They're arranged opposite each other on the stem, and each leaflet has serrated edges that feel slightly prickly when you run your finger along them.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright, bushy plants that grow from thick, fleshy underground tubers. Stems are hollow and can feel surprisingly sturdy but will snap crisply when bent. Plants branch freely, creating full, rounded shapes in the garden.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Thick, succulent-like stems that are completely hollow inside - you can hear them rattle if seeds get inside. The stems are usually green to reddish-green and feel smooth but sturdy, though they're quite brittle and break easily.

habitat: Garden dahlias are found exclusively in cultivated settings throughout New England - flower gardens, borders, and sometimes escaped near old homesteads. They thrive in rich, well-drained soil in full sun locations. Since they can't survive our winters outdoors, you'll only see them during the growing season where gardeners have planted them or where tubers have been stored and replanted.

seasonality.spring: Not visible - tubers are either stored indoors or just being planted. Gardeners typically plant dahlia tubers after the last frost date when soil has warmed.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing and blooming season. Plants emerge in early summer and begin blooming mid to late summer, producing flowers continuously until frost. This is when identification is easiest.
seasonality.fall: Continue blooming profusely until the first hard frost kills the above-ground portions. The contrast of bright dahlia blooms against fall foliage is spectacular but brief.
seasonality.winter: Completely dormant with no above-ground presence. Tubers must be dug and stored indoors in New England, or they'll freeze and die in our cold winters.

funFact: Dahlia tubers were originally eaten as a food crop by the Aztecs, and when they first arrived in Europe, people kept trying to eat them instead of growing them for their flowers - it took decades before Europeans figured out that dahlias were much better as eye candy than actual candy!
confusionNotes: Garden dahlias might be confused with cosmos or zinnias from a distance, but dahlia leaves are distinctively divided into leaflets while cosmos and zinnias have simple, undivided leaves. Remember: 'Dahlia leaves are divided' - the alliteration helps you remember this key difference.
contextualKnowledge: Though called 'garden dahlia,' these are actually complex hybrids (Dahlia × pinnata) rather than a pure species. They're tender perennials that must be treated as annuals in New England's climate unless gardeners dig up and store the tubers each winter - a practice that connects modern gardeners to centuries of dahlia cultivation.
compareHints: Since garden dahlia is the only dahlia species commonly grown in New England, compare it to other members of the sunflower family. Unlike sunflowers, dahlias have divided leaves and hollow stems. Unlike asters, dahlias bloom much larger and their leaves are compound rather than simple, plus they lack the late-season timing of wild asters.
